title: The King Who Spared the Ox
text:
King Xuan of Qi asked Mencius whether someone like him could become a true king who protects his people. Mencius said yes, and gave a reason. He had heard that the king, sitting in his hall, once saw an ox being led past. The animal was to be killed so its blood could consecrate a new bell. The king could not bear to watch it trembling like an innocent man going to execution, and ordered it released and a sheep used instead.

The king admitted it was true. His people, he said, thought he had done it out of stinginess, swapping a big animal for a small one. Mencius said he knew better: the king had seen the ox and not the sheep. The feeling that moved him was real compassion, and that feeling was enough to make a true king.

Then Mencius pressed his point. The king's kindness was enough to reach animals, yet its benefits did not reach his people. A man who could lift a heavy weight but claimed he could not lift a feather was not unable, only unwilling. The king's failure to care for his people was the same: not that he could not, but that he did not. He needed only to extend the heart he already had from the ox in front of him to everyone in his kingdom.
lesson: Most of us already feel care for the people right in front of us. The work of leadership is to extend that same care to those you do not see every day.
